newsitem.title: USA: Dow leaps past 7,500 mark, other stocks end mixed.
newsitem.headline: Dow leaps past 7,500 mark, other stocks end mixed.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average roared past yet another milestone on Tuesday, closing above the 7,500-point level for the first time in its history.

The Dow gained rose 60.77 to 7,539.27, the third straight record finish for blue chips. The broad market turned in a mixed performance, however, with stocks in technology and transportation companies slumping.
Advancers outpaced decliners 1,404 to 1,131 on heavy volume of almost 527 million on the New York Stock Exchange.
Analysts said the continuing rally among top-tier stocks reflects a market that remains awash in cash, although several noted the source of that cash appears to have changed.
In the past, mutual fund inflows have generally been cited as the key contributor to the stock market's relentless climb.
Analysts said the rally now appeared to be developing an international flavor amid mounting political and economic questions over the future of European Monetary Union (EMU).

"It seems like, suddenly, we have all these questions about whether EMU will be delayed or whether we will be facing a much-weakened European currency," said Jack Shaughnessy, director of research at Advest.

"If you look at the stocks in the Dow that were up today, like Boeing and Caterpillar and Chevron, these are the kinds of internationally recognised names that foreign investors tend to buy," he said.

Shares in Boeing Co. gained 1-1/2 to 57-1/2 after the company announced it had signed several major aircraft sale contracts. Caterpillar Inc. gained 1-3/4 to 103-5/8 and Chevron Corp. rose 1-1/2 to 73-3/8.
Beyond the fairly narrow advance by blue chips, the market lacked the vigour displayed in recent sessions. Several groups met with selling pressure amid concerns about upcoming earnings.

Airline stocks were one such group, with American Airlines parent company AMR Corp. falling 4-5/8 to 94-1/2 and Delta Air Lines Inc. down 3-3/4 to 88. On Monday, Delta warned that revenues for its current fiscal quarter would show only a slight improvement from year-ago levels.
The Nasdaq Composite index fell 10.35 points to 1,401.69, snapping its three-session winning streak as several networking and semiconductor equipment stocks tumbled.
Still, analysts said the selling pressure was narrowly targeted, a sign investors remain firmly committed to stocks and content to simply shift funds from one group to the next.
With the Dow now above 7,500, and already well past many strategists' targets for the year, the main fear among investors seems to be of missing out on the next advance.

"For the third year in a row now, we have managed to prove the experts too conservative," said Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross. "We've gotten to the point where it's a panic to get invested."
During such periods, analysts said, worries about interest rates and earnings seem to temporarily fade.
"The bottom line right now is that the market doesn't seem to be worried about much of anything," said Barbara Marcin, vice president at Citibank Global Asset Management.

Among individual issues, Santa Fe International Corp. jumped 3-1/2 to 32 in the contract driller's first day of trading. Santa Fe's initial public offering, which raised about $997.5 million, was the largest so far this year.
BDM International Inc. skidded 6-3/4 to 20-3/4 after the company warned its second-quarter earnings would be well below Wall Street estimates.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks rose 2.36 points to 865.27, a record. The American Stock Exchange index added 1.54 to 621.11.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 1.59 to 451.76, a record. The average price per share rose 15 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues also known as the Wilshire 5000 -- was a record 8,194.766, up 14.529 or 0.18 percent.
